title: Viscosity Dominance and Global Regularity for the Forced Three-Dimensional Navier–Stokes Equations
content: We consider the Cauchy problem for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with an external force written in divergence form, \(f=\operatorname{div}G\). We give a short, self-contained proof at the \(H^1\) level that the solution is global, smooth and unique whenever the product \(E_0Y_0\) of the energy-level data \((v_0, G)\) and the enstrophy-level data \((\nabla v_0, f)\) is smaller than \(\frac{27}{256\pi^4}v^4\approx0.642^4 v^4\). The condition is invariant under the scaling of the equations and gives one explicit sufficient form of the statement that viscosity dominates the force. It implies the classical small-data condition in the critical space \(\dot H^{1/2}\), so the result belongs to the Fujita-Kato theory; its contribution is the elementary proof, the sharp-constant threshold and the divergence-form treatment of the force. We also record the classical local existence time with an explicit constant. As a corollary, every finite-energy solution that becomes singular under a smooth force, in particular the forced construction announced by OpenAI in 2026 if it is correct, must violate the condition, which gives an explicit lower bound on the force. The second part of the paper develops a complementary estimate of a different nature. Treating the velocity components as potentials of the Schr\"odinger operator, we use the author's representation of the potential through the scattering data, obtained from the Poincar\'e-Riemann-Hilbert problem in the absence of a discrete spectrum. We put the representation into the normalized form required by the Riemann-Hilbert problem and fix its constants by the Born approximation. The operator of the Schr\"odinger equation then removes the Cauchy kernel from the first term exactly, and this term becomes the inverse fixed-angle Born approximation, which reproduces the potential exactly at first order. We correct the normalization, the constant of the jump operator and the smallness condition of the earlier formulation (replacing it by the scale-invariant Kato norm). We also explain why, with the velocity used as a potential with a free coupling constant, this representation cannot by itself give information beyond Fourier analysis of the velocity. What it would need is an independent estimate of its nonlinear part through the scattering data, and this remains open. Finally, we replace the free coupling by the scale-invariant potential \(-c|v|^2/r^2\) and show, via an \(\varepsilon\)-regularity criterion of Gustafson, Kang and Tsai and the Birman-Schwinger principle, that every finite-time singularity of a finite-energy solution under a smooth, compactly supported force makes this potential bind (produce a negative eigenvalue) along times approaching the singular time, for every coupling above a universal but non-explicit threshold. For unforced flows, using the enstrophy balance instead, we show with the explicit coupling \(c=1\) that the binding times have measure at least \(4\pi^4/v^3\|\nabla v(t)\|^4\) in every interval \((t,T^*)\); here the absence of bound states is exactly the bound \(m(v)\leq v\) on the multiplier norm of \(v\) from \(H^1\) to \(L^2\) (a classical equivalence). With a force, binding on a set of times of positive measure holds for every coupling \(c>1\). For unforced flows the potential binds at every time before the singularity, for every coupling above another non-explicit threshold; equivalently, the absence of bound states at one time, for one such coupling, implies global regularity; moreover, for every \(\theta>0\) and every coupling above a threshold depending on \(\theta\), the ground-state energy of an unforced singular solution satisfies \(E_1(t)\leq-\theta/(v(t^* - t))\), a spectral analogue of Leray's lower bound. For smooth compactly supported forces the existence of bound states and this bound hold on a final time interval before the singularity, and for unforced type I singularities the number of bound states near the singular time is at least the number of singular points, for couplings above a threshold depending on the type I constant. In kinematic model scenarios, self-similar profiles keep the number of bound states fixed, while faster-than-self-similar amplitude growth makes it tend to infinity.
